sections.title: Build your introduction from four lines
body: Copy whole chunks before studying grammar: Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar … Say Jag heter Alex. Mitt namn är Alex is correct too, but it sounds like filling in a form.

The slip beginners make most: mixing two boxes. Jag bor i tells where you live now. Jag kommer från tells where you come from. Join them with men (but): Jag kommer från Indien, men jag bor i Helsingfors nu.

The first sound of every chunk: Swedish J is always the y in yes (Hindi य), never the j in jam (ज). Jag sounds like yaag, ja like yaa. Hindi written in English letters uses j for ज (jaldi), so this slip comes easily.

In Swedish, use the Swedish names of places in Finland: Helsingfors (Helsinki), Esbo (Espoo), Vanda (Vantaa), Åbo (Turku). Helsingfors is stressed at the end: hel-sing-FORS. The Finnish name HEL-sin-ki pulls you to the start.

Use och before the last language, with no comma before och (English often puts one there). Put lite directly before each language you speak only a little, as your teacher did: Jag talar engelska, svenska, lite ryska och lite portugisiska. Language names take a small letter: hindi, svenska.

examples.note: Replace Alex with your own name. Jag starts with a y sound.
Your home now. Helsingfors is the Swedish name for Helsinki; stress the end: hel-sing-FORS.

sections.title: Nine vowels: copy the mouth first
body: The Swedish alphabet is the English one plus three letters at the end: å, ä, ö (29 letters; a dictionary lists them after z). Swedish has nine vowel letters: A, O, U, Y, I, E, Ö, Ä, Å. First copy the lip and tongue position; then copy the audio.
English, Hindi, and Marathi examples are memory bridges, not exact Swedish pronunciation. The Swedish recording is the final model.

Two surprises for a Hindi speaker: Swedish O usually sounds close to ऊ (bok, bor), and the ओ sound you know is usually written Å (från, hår). U, Y and Ö have no Hindi or Marathi match. If you have heard Finnish around Helsinki, Finnish y, ö and ä are close to the Swedish ones.
Rounded lips: O, U, Y, Ö, Å. Front tongue: I, E, Y, Ä, Ö. Notice that Y and Ö belong to both groups.

sections.title: Long or short: stretch one part
body: Stress first: most Swedish words are stressed on the first syllable (SVEN-ska, MAM-ma, IN-di-en). Loanwords often keep a late stress (ka-FÉ, pa-ra-PLY), and so does your city: hel-sing-FORS. Stress and length help people understand you more than a perfect vowel does.
In a stressed Swedish syllable, either the vowel is long or the consonant after it is long. Hear both parts, not only the vowel.

A common spelling clue is: one consonant letter after the stressed vowel often means a longer vowel; a doubled consonant often means a short vowel and longer consonant. Your teacher's English bridge works the same way: write (long i) and written (short i before tt). It is a clue, not a rule without exceptions.
Use the routine: find the stressed vowel → look right → listen → copy the whole word.

examples.note: Stretch the a in tak; stop it quickly and hold the k in tack.
Stress moves: ka-FÉ (a loanword) but KAF-fe, with a short a and a long f.
Bor has a long stressed vowel; the doubled consonants signal short stressed vowels in the other words.

activity.summary: One consonant after the stressed vowel usually means stretch. Two consonants usually mean stop. It is a strong clue, not a law, so the recording always has the final say.

sections.title: One vowel group, three soft sounds
body: The spelling group E, I, Y, Ä, Ö often softens the consonant immediately before it. These are front vowels because the tongue is forward; Y and Ö still use rounded lips. The softening happens mainly at the start of a word or a stressed syllable; later in a word the consonant often stays hard, as the k in pojke (boy).
G usually becomes the Swedish j sound, K usually becomes the tj sound /ɕ/, and SK usually becomes the sj sound /ɧ/ before this group.

Two accents, both correct. In Finland-Swedish, the Swedish you hear in Helsinki, tj sounds close to ch in chai (your teacher's ciao) and sj sounds close to English sh (श). The app's voices are from Sweden: their tj is a soft hiss with no t, and their sj is a breathier, rounder sound. Copy whichever you hear around you; people understand both.
Use the shortcut to predict, then use audio to learn the actual sound. Some loanwords are exceptions. One habit to avoid: do not put an i before sk, as in iskärm. Say skärm, ska, skuld straight away.

examples.note: The first vowel is Ä or I.

activity.label: Sound detective
activity.title: Look at the letter after g, k, or sk, then predict the sound
activity.instructions: Swedish teachers call e, i, y, ä, ö the soft vowels (mjuka vokaler) and a, o, u, å the hard vowels (hårda vokaler). Soft vowel next? The consonant usually softens too. Hard vowel next? It stays hard. Choose, then listen.

K + i, a front vowel: the soft tj sound.
A is a back vowel, so sk stays hard: s + k.
Sk + ä, a front vowel: the sj sound.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
A is a back vowel, so k stays hard.
K + ö: Ö is rounded but still a front vowel, so k softens.
Sj is always the sj sound, whatever vowel follows.

activity.summary: One question does most of the work: which vowel comes next? Front vowels (e, i, y, ä, ö) soften g, k and sk into three different sounds; back vowels leave them hard. Sj, skj and tj keep their sound whatever follows. Some loanwords break the rule, so trust the recording.

sections.title: Recognise the remaining Lesson 1 spellings
body: Recognition only today: SJ and SKJ normally use the sj sound, as in sjuk and skjorta. At the start of a word, HJ, DJ and LJ are said as the Swedish j alone: hjälp sounds like yelp, djur like yoor, ljus like yoos.

RS is where the two accents differ. In Sweden the r melts into the s, giving a sh made with the tongue tip curled back, as for Hindi ट or ड. That is your teacher's sh in kurs and mars. Finland-Swedish usually keeps R + S separate, so in Helsinki you hear hel-sing-FORS, while the app's Sweden voices say something closer to hel-sing-FOSH. Both are correct.

Plain Swedish t and d are dental, like Hindi त and द: the tongue touches the back of the top teeth. Say tack with त, not with the ट that Indian English often uses for t. Good news for Helsinki: Finland-Swedish says t and k without a puff of air, like your plain त and क, and rolls or taps r much like Hindi र. The app's Sweden voices add a small puff of air after t and k, and their r is softer.
Och is /ɔk/ in careful speech and often just å in conversation.

examples.note: Two spellings for the sj sound.
Initial H or L is silent in these spellings; begin with Swedish j.
The d is silent: say yoor, with the Swedish long u.
Sweden: one curled-tongue sh. Finland-Swedish: r + s kept apart. Choose one and be consistent.

examples.note: The textbook uses skönt hår; fint hår is the natural compliment to produce.

assignment.title: Episode 1 mission: Say who you are
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say your real four-line introduction once slowly and once at normal speed: name, home now, origin, and languages.

ONE SOUND LOOP: Choose only one: tak/tack OR gillar/kött/skärm. Listen and repeat the small set three times.

RETURN: Close the model and give your real introduction from memory in under 20 seconds.
assignment.model:
Hej! Jag heter Alex.
Jag bor i Helsingfors.
Jag kommer från Indien.
Jag talar hindi, engelska och lite svenska.

takeaways: Core: say Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar … as four complete chunks.
Two boxes: bor i = home now, kommer från = origin. Join them with men: … men jag bor i Helsingfors nu.
Swedish j is always य, the y in yes: jag = yaag. Stress your city at the end: hel-sing-FORS.
Mouth first, audio second: use the Hindi/Marathi/English bridge to find the shape, then copy the Swedish model.
Practise one contrast at a time: tak/tack or the g → j, k → tj, sk → sj pattern.
Two accents, both correct: in Helsinki tj sounds like ch and sj like sh; the app's Sweden voices say them more softly.

pronunciation.text: Jag. Ja. Bok. Bor. Du. Dum. By. Paraply. Le. Ö. Bär. Från. Tak. Tack. Gäst. Gillar. Kina. Kött. Skärm. Skiner. Sjuk. Skjorta. Kurs. Mars. Hjälp. Djur. Ljus.
pronunciation.tip: Do not repeat the whole list at once. Choose one group: the nine vowel words, tak/tack, or gillar/kött/skärm. Every j is the y in yes (य), so hjälp, djur and ljus start with that y. For kurs and mars, the voice uses the Sweden sound; Finland-Swedish keeps r + s apart.

Hälsningar, Noor

gist.prompt: Your classmate Noor posted this in the class group chat. What is it?
gist.explanation: Hej alla! opens it, Noor gives a name, origin, home and languages, and Hälsningar closes it: a hello to the class.

detail.explanation: Men jag bor i Esbo nu: but I live in Espoo now. Pakistan is where Noor comes from (kommer från).

reading.text:
Hej alla!
Jag heter Noor. Jag kommer från Pakistan, men jag bor i Esbo nu.
Jag talar urdu, engelska och lite svenska.
Hälsningar, Noor
reading.question: Which language does Noor speak only a little?
reading.explanation: Lite svenska: a little Swedish. Lite stands directly before that language.

listening.text: Hej! Jag heter Elin. Jag kommer från Vasa, men jag bor i Helsingfors nu. Jag talar svenska, finska och engelska. Och du? Var kommer du ifrån?
listening.question: Elin names two cities. Where does she come from?
listening.explanation: Jag kommer från Vasa: she comes from Vaasa. Men jag bor i Helsingfors nu: she lives in Helsinki now. Kommer från = origin; bor i = home now.

speaking.prompt: YKI-style interview, theme: you. Answer the four questions in full sentences: name, home now, origin and languages.
speaking.help: The interviewer asks: Vad heter du? Var bor du? Var kommer du ifrån? Vilka språk talar du? Answer: Hej! Jag heter … Jag bor i … Jag kommer från … Jag talar … och lite svenska. YKI asks you to talk actively (Försök tala aktivt!), so answer with a full sentence, not one word.
speaking.model: Hej! Jag heter Alex. Jag bor i Helsingfors. Jag kommer från Indien. Jag talar hindi, engelska och lite svenska.

writing.prompt: Write a short message to your new class: who you are, where you live, where you come from, and what you speak.
writing.situation: You have joined a Swedish class in Helsingfors. The teacher asks everyone to write a short hello to the class group chat. A YKI writing task looks like this too: a short message, a few points to cover, and a proper start and end.
points: Greet the class and say your name.
Say which languages you speak, and which one only a little.
End with a greeting and your name.
writing.help: Hej alla! (Hi everyone!) · Jag heter … · Jag kommer från …, men jag bor i … nu. · Jag talar … och lite svenska. · End with Hälsningar (Best wishes) and your name. YKI always checks that a message opens and closes properly (in Swedish the task says: Kom ihåg att inleda och avsluta meddelandet).
writing.model:
Hej alla!
Jag heter Alex. Jag kommer från Indien, men jag bor i Helsingfors nu.
Jag talar hindi, engelska och lite svenska.
Hälsningar, Alex

route.expectedOutput: Say a clear four-line introduction with your real details, then write it as a short message to your class.
route.transferPrompt: Say it again with one change: join origin and home in one sentence with men … nu (Jag kommer från …, men jag bor i … nu).
route.returnPrompt: From memory, in under 20 seconds: your name, origin and home joined with men, and your languages.
successChecks: Answer in full sentences: Jag heter, Jag bor i, Jag kommer från, Jag talar.
Keep home now (bor i) and origin (kommer från) apart.
Start jag with a y sound (य), and stress hel-sing-FORS at the end.
Speak once with your plan and once without looking.
